clue.text: Deception to end nap, that is for wee one in nursery?

parts.note: to kid is to deceive, and a kid is a hoax
to die is to come to an end
a wink of sleep, as in forty winks
the abbreviation of id est

explanation.surface: A trick to cut short a toddler's nap in the nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' is Scots for small; the question mark nods to the other sense of wee and to nursery as a place for young plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiddiewinkie is a jocular word for a small child, the kind looked after in a nursery.

clue.text: Sober duke, festal possibly, ready to set off with hunt?

definitions.text: ready to set off with hunt?

indicators.note: possibly says the word before it is only one way its letters might be arranged

parts.note: sad in its old sense of steady, serious
D is the abbreviation for duke
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A duke who stays sober despite the festivities is ready to ride out with the hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Sad once meant sober or staid, which is how it serves here.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sitting firmly in the saddle is mounted and secure, so ready to go off hunting; the question mark admits the definition is loose.

clue.text: Take parts lower in old inventory

indicators.note: parts here is a verb: one piece splits the other by sitting in its middle

parts.note: to lower, pronounced to rhyme with flower, is to frown
R stands for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: An instruction to take some parts down to a lower level, found in an old list.
explanation.walkthrough: Lower here rhymes with power and means to frown, not to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrowl is an obsolete spelling of scroll, which once meant a written list or schedule, an inventory.

clue.text: One who hesitates to bet with buck around?

indicators.note: around means the animal is placed on both sides of the other piece

parts.note: a buck is a male deer
to lay a bet is to wager

explanation.surface: A cautious gambler who wavers before betting on a horse with a stag nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Buck looks like slang for a dollar, a stake; it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A delayer puts off acting, so is someone who hesitates.

clue.text: Road up, stages reset to include run for racing cars

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: RD is the standard abbreviation for road

indicators.note: to include means taking in another piece
reset means set again in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: With the road dug up, race stages are rearranged to add a run for the cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Dragsters are cars built for drag racing, sprinting over a short straight course.

clue.text: Billed artistes almost feebly given lift receiving minimum of éclat

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the word means writing it from bottom to top
receiving means taking another letter inside
almost means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: punily means weakly

indicators.note: the minimum of a word is the smallest part one can take, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Performers on the bill, weak and needing a boost, show barely any flair.
explanation.definitionFit: The line-up is the list of performers billed to appear at a show or festival.

clue.text: Odd bits? Sidonie's turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top
odd picks the letters in odd-numbered places: first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: letters one, three, five and seven

explanation.surface: Sidonie's odds and sods have reappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd bits' does double duty: it picks the odd letters and, with the question mark, defines leftover scraps, odds and ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends are leftover scraps, as in odds and ends, so odd bits.

clue.text: Being aligned, one's first war goes amiss

indicators.note: goes amiss means goes wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order
first keeps only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lines up, and their first war goes badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Arow is an old word, used by Spenser, meaning in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Arow is an archaic adverb meaning in a row, one after another, so in alignment.

clue.text: Those born to immigrant parents without East Indian sons

parts.note: sans is French for without, used in English
E is the compass abbreviation
I is an abbreviation for Indian
S is short for sons, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Children of incomers, born to families with no sons from the Indian subcontinent.
explanation.walkthrough: Sansei is Japanese for third generation; the plural here takes an English s.
explanation.definitionFit: Sansei are North Americans of Japanese descent, the children of nisei and grandchildren of the original immigrants.

clue.text: We'll never darken your doorstep, honest, dressed in a suit!

indicators.note: in places the reshaped word inside the card suit

parts.note: one of the four suits in a pack of cards

indicators.note: dressed is used as stone is dressed, worked into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Smartly dressed visitors promise, honestly, that they will never call on you again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never darken your door' is a parting vow never to visit, but the speakers are the soft stones once rubbed on doorsteps to whiten them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearthstones were blocks of soft stone used to scour and whiten steps, so they only ever lightened a doorstep.

clue.text: Wherein graddan first grew, part of rustic kernel

indicators.note: part of says only a portion of the following words is wanted, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A rustic note on where grain first grew, from part of the kernel.
explanation.walkthrough: Graddan is Scots for parched grain; an icker is the Scots word for an ear of corn, where that grain grew.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear of corn holds the grain before it is parched into graddan, so it is where the grain grew.

clue.text: One gets reverse of thanks in turbulent reign … from such a one?

definitions.text: One gets reverse of thanks in turbulent reign … from such a one?

indicators.note: reverse of asks for the word that follows to be read from its last letter back to its first
in places one piece inside the letters of another
turbulent suggests disorder, so the following word's letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: A ruler in troubled times receives the opposite of gratitude, from an ungrateful subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the turned-round thanks sits inside the jumbled reign, and the reverse of thanks is just what you get from an ungrateful person.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, someone from whom you receive the opposite of thanks.

clue.text: Thomas maybe catching start of rabies then died — not the drink (7, two words)

indicators.note: catching means the name grabs and holds another piece within it

parts.note: Dylan Thomas, the Welsh poet; maybe flags him as one Thomas among many

indicators.note: start of keeps only the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: Thomas caught rabies and died, apparently without touching a drop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea, so 'not the drink' is land rather than water; the drinking surface points at Dylan Thomas's famous thirst.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink is informal for the sea, and dry land is ground as opposed to water.

clue.text: 'Very good' — where you may hear that tucking into snake

indicators.note: tucking into means one piece goes inside another, as food goes into a mouth

parts.note: the boa is a constricting snake
New Zealand, where this slang praise is heard

explanation.surface: Someone praises a snake's meal, noting where such praise is heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' refers back to the definition: the word is Australasian slang, so New Zealand is where you would hear it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonza is Australian and New Zealand slang for excellent, first-rate.

clue.text: Element, not alas for gypsy women

indicators.note: not means leave out the word that follows it

parts.note: zincala is a Spanish Romany word for a gypsy woman; for marks the word that loses letters
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: An element mourned by gypsy women, minus the lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Zinc is a metallic chemical element, number 30.

clue.text: 'Life's last scene' — quotation in John?

parts.note: surface reading: a line from a play about a death scene
setter's reading: the quoted phrase illustrates a word in a dictionary such as Johnson's, and the word it illustrates is old age's last stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'John?' hints at Samuel Johnson, whose dictionary illustrated each word with quotations; the phrase calls to mind Jaques's 'Last scene of all ... second childishness' in As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotage is the feeble-minded final stage of old age, the closing scene of a life.

clue.text: Shakespearean most properly present in dissemination of arts

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the second
dissemination scatters things, so the letters of the next word are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
there in the sense of present, in attendance

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean actor, most properly present when the arts are spread abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Ratherest is used once by Shakespeare, in Love's Labour's Lost, as a superlative of rather.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's ratherest is glossed as most especially or most properly, a superlative of rather.

clue.text: Moving unsteadily back, pair ending up splits — it includes telephone links

indicators.note: back asks for what remains to be read from right to left
the two letters at the close of the word break away and are dropped

parts.note: yawing is swinging off course, as a ship or aircraft does

explanation.surface: Someone lurching backwards splits a pair of phone lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The I-way is short for the information superhighway, the network that includes telephone links; losing its last two letters turns yawing into yawi before the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: The I-way, or information superhighway, is the communications network built on cable and telephone connections.

clue.text: Junior rep maybe busting gut with beans

indicators.note: busting means bursting apart, so the letters come out in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young sales representative overeats beans until his stomach bursts.
explanation.definitionFit: A subagent works under a main agent, so is a junior representative; maybe marks it as one example.

clue.text: Coarse tow: the whole lot I cut short mostly from below

indicators.note: in a down clue, from below means read from bottom to top
mostly means not all of it, so the last letter goes

parts.note: all is the whole lot
taken as written
to dock is to cut short, as a tail is docked

explanation.surface: Rough rope fibre: the speaker trimmed the whole lot from underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: Tow is the broken fibre of flax or hemp, not towing.
explanation.definitionFit: Codilla is the coarsest part of the tow of flax or hemp, the short broken fibre.

clue.text: Noisy old bird, ample after stone's put on

indicators.note: after says the word before it comes second, following the weight named next

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the weight
rich in the sense of plentiful

explanation.surface: A loud old bird, quite plump once a stone has been put on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ample after stone's put on' tells you the stone goes in front. Strich is Spenser's word for the screech owl.
explanation.definitionFit: The strich is an archaic name for the screech owl, a bird known for its harsh cry.

clue.text: Form of iron e.g. cobbler inserted as reinforcement

indicators.note: inserted means put inside another piece
form of suggests a different shape made from the same letters

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a cobbler is a fruit pie with a scone topping

explanation.surface: An iron shoe-plate that a cobbler fits to strengthen a boot.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobbler looks like a shoe-mender, which suits iron and reinforcement; here it is the baked dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripieno is the full body of supporting players in baroque music, who reinforce the solo group.

clue.text: Spent time with tarts, a great number we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the answer is a word that sounds like the wordplay when spoken

parts.note: a hoard is a large store or quantity

explanation.surface: Someone spent time with women of easy virtue, a great many of them apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Tarts here are prostitutes, not pastries.
explanation.definitionFit: To whore is to consort with prostitutes, so the past tense means having spent time in their company.

clue.text: Plain American husband — aw gee!

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
O my, an exclamation of mild surprise

explanation.surface: A plain-spoken American husband exclaims in surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Homy, or homey, is American usage for homely in the sense of plain or unattractive.

clue.text: Taxes wine taken on board ship

indicators.note: taken on board means carried inside the vessel

parts.note: SS is short for steamship
tent is a deep red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: Duties are levied on wine loaded aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent is a Spanish red wine once used at communion.
explanation.definitionFit: Stent is a Scots word for an assessment or tax, so stents are taxes.

clue.text: Right to commandeer stuff in war — one storehouse ran out

definitions.text: Right to commandeer stuff in war

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, one

indicators.note: out means removed from the word it belongs to

parts.note: a granary stores grain
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: In wartime one storehouse has been emptied by requisitioning.
explanation.definitionFit: Angary is the right of a warring state to seize or use neutral property, subject to paying compensation.

clue.text: Medicinal powder, i.e. boxes I do try when taken poorly

indicators.note: boxes means encloses, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: taken as written, the abbreviation for that is

indicators.note: taken poorly suggests something out of sorts, so the letters fall into a different order

parts.note: the six letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a medicinal powder for when you are feeling ill.
explanation.walkthrough: Iodyrite is native silver iodide, a yellowish mineral; the clue treats it as a medicinal powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Iodyrite is silver iodide occurring naturally, a compound once used in medicine as a powder.

clue.text: Public fountain in Glasgow? Rubbish is seen in more than one of them

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dialect word, used in northern Britain, for a public drinking fountain

definitions.text: Rubbish is seen in more than one of them
definitions.meaning: second meaning: put the word in the plural and you have British slang for rubbish

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a playful definition: 'pants' is British slang for rubbish, so rubbish shows up when there is more than one of these.
explanation.definitionFit: In northern British dialect the word names a public well or fountain, and its plural is slang for nonsense.

clue.text: It's no good leaving very hot shellfish

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: as in piping hot
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A seafood warning that it is no good letting the shellfish get too hot.
explanation.definitionFit: The pipi is an edible bivalve mollusc of Australian and New Zealand beaches.

clue.text: Bill gets out of bed, and likewise out of risqué spot

indicators.note: gets out of means leaves, so those letters are removed

parts.note: the sack is slang for bed
racy means saucy, risqué
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A man gets out of bed and likewise out of a compromising situation.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill is the account, not a man, and the same two letters come out of both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Skry is an old word meaning to descry, to catch sight of, so to spot.

clue.text: Old-style candied confection the disciplined ignore

indicators.note: disciplined suggests letters brought into order, a fresh arrangement of the word that follows

parts.note: the six letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sweet from the old days that people with self-control pass over.
explanation.walkthrough: Eringo, also spelt eryngo, is the candied root of sea holly, a sweetmeat Shakespeare mentions.
explanation.definitionFit: Eringo is sea-holly root preserved in sugar, a candied sweetmeat popular in earlier centuries.

clue.text: Drinking cup I was last to drink my fill, one over the eight

indicators.note: last keeps only the final letter of each of the words that follow

parts.note: the final letter of each of the three words
nine in Roman numerals, one more than eight

explanation.surface: A drinker boasts of being last to finish, one over the eight, which means tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for drunk, but here it means nine, IX. The words 'I was' serve the surface; the wordplay does not use them.
explanation.definitionFit: A kylix is a shallow two-handled cup on a stem from ancient Greece, used for drinking wine.

clue.text: Bone, if cut from blade, fashioned a pen

indicators.note: cut from means the first piece is removed from the second

parts.note: a knife is a blade
taken as written, the letters to remove

indicators.note: fashioned means made into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the four letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shaped a pen out of a bone, perhaps by cutting it with a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneepan is another name for the kneecap or patella, the bone at the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: What's in this? Unfavourably I shall separate (7, two words)

parts.note: I'll is the contraction of I shall
to part is to separate

explanation.surface: A puzzled question and then a stiff declaration that the speaker will leave on bad terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's in this?' asks for the phrase that follows 'in' in an idiom: 'in ill part' means unfavourably, as in taking a remark in ill part.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something in ill part is an idiom for receiving it with offence, that is unfavourably.

clue.text: Rout at Bannockburn a very long time back — king involved

indicators.note: back asks for the phrase before it to be read from right to left
involved means caught up inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: eons are vast ages
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Seems to recall Robert the Bruce's 1314 defeat of the English at Bannockburn, long ago, with a king at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Rout looks like a military defeat, but 'at Bannockburn' marks it as Scots, where rout means to snore or bellow.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, to rout is to roar or snore, so the Scots verb gives the ordinary word for noisy breathing in sleep.

clue.text: Porky created by young, taking in jaunty drunken sot

indicators.note: a drunken walk is unsteady and disordered, so the letters of the word after it are jumbled
taking in means holding other pieces inside

parts.note: fry are young fish
airy in the sense of light-hearted
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A tall tale invented by a youngster about a cheerful drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Porky is rhyming slang: porky pie, a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairy story is an untruth told as fact, which is what a porky, a lie, is.
